# Organizational Effectiveness: Innovation [507]

Page 507 is the Innovation divider. This group has two measures.

| Measure | Book page |
|---|---|
| New Products & Services Revenue per FTE | 508 |
| R&D Expense Rate | 510 |

: Innovation measures {.striped}

## New Products & Services Revenue per FTE [508-509]

| Item | Summary |
|---|---|
| Icons | Cost, Ratio; Bench-H, Data-H |
| Application | Organizations trying to grow revenue or market share, or shift their customer base, through new products and services |
| Description | Average operating revenue from new products and services per FTE |
| Sourcing | Financial data assigned by product line. The product lines counted as "new" must be defined, and this varies with industry development cycles and product shelf lives |

: Profile summary {.striped}

$$\text{New Products \& Services Revenue per FTE} = \frac{\text{Operating Revenue.New Products \& Services}}{\text{FTE}}$$

**Reading it.** Shows revenue from new products and services relative to workforce size, as a subset of operating revenue. It is a lagging indicator of how well product development and innovation work, and successes and failures give lessons for future launches. Comparing new-product revenue with other revenue also shows the learning curve for sales, customer service, and other staff. Some launches barely disturb customer-facing staff, while others need heavy training and disrupt productivity. Knowing the likely scale helps plan training, recruiting, pay, and engagement programs.

**Analysis.** By individual new product or product area, to see where new revenue comes from. Also by organizational unit, division, or geography to compare launch success.

**Limitations.** Does not show revenue from older products, the length of the development cycle, the investment needed for a launch, or market share and competitiveness.

**Targets.** Based on product mix, how often new products launch, and adoption cycles in the industry. Targets may stay steady if launches are frequent, or spike and drop if rare. Benchmark targets depend on product-introduction strategy and the strength of existing products.

**Variations.** New Products & Services Revenue per FTE—New Geographies; —New Markets; —New Products; —New Services.

**Related measures.** Market Capitalization per FTE; Net Hire Ratio; New Position Recruitment Rate; Operating Profit per FTE; Operating Revenue per FTE; Organization Tenure Staffing Breakdown; R&D Expense Rate; Staffing Rate—Customer Facing; Staffing Rate—Multilingual; Staffing Rate—Revenue Generating; Staffing Rate—Temporary; Training Course Content Breakdown; Work Units per FTE.

## R&D Expense Rate [510-511]

| Item | Summary |
|---|---|
| Icons | Cost, Rate; Bench-M, Data-M |
| Application | Industries that depend on research and development for long-term product viability, such as many technology and manufacturing sectors |
| Description | Research and development (R&D) expense as a share of total operating expense |
| Sourcing | Financial statements under generally accepted accounting principles, ledger accounts, or electronic versions of statements |

: Profile summary {.striped}

$$\text{R\&D Expense Rate} = \frac{\text{R\&D Expense}}{\text{Operating Expense}} \times 100$$

**Reading it.** A result of 20% means R&D was 20% of operating expense. In some industries R&D is a leading indicator of future product lines. Some sectors must keep investing just to hold their position, while elsewhere it signals a temporary push on a new or updated line. Understanding R&D emphasis helps anticipate product and market change and plan the workforce. R&D spend should follow a product-improvement strategy, which drives human capital strategy, so the rate can signal workforce growth needs.

**Analysis.** By product line, organizational unit, or geography, to see how R&D investment varies.

**Limitations.** Does not show the total amount spent on R&D, only its share of expense. It does not show the quality or fit of R&D investment for future success, or the workforce needs it creates.

**Targets.** Based on R&D strategy. Organizations using R&D as a competitive differentiator will likely aim for the 75th percentile of a group in similar industries. Others may aim for the median or lower. Absolute targets are also likely, based on budgets and product plans.

**Variations.** R&D Expense Rate—New Products; R&D Expense Rate—Redesign.

**Related measures.** Average Number of Options per Employee; Function Staffing Breakdown; Intangible Asset Value per FTE; Market Compensation Ratio; New Products & Services Revenue per FTE; Operating Expense per FTE; Operating Revenue per FTE; Organization Tenure Staffing Breakdown; Staffing Rate—Customer Facing; Staffing Rate—Graduate Degree; Training Course Content Breakdown; Training Hours per FTE; Work Units per FTE.
